content: The implementation of point-of-care tests (POCTs) for syphilis screening in pregnant women across six lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) demonstrated significant improvements in testing and treatment outcomes. In Brazil, no prior syphilis screening was conducted, while in China, rapid plasma reagin (RPR) tests were confirmed with Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay (TPPA). In Peru, Uganda, Tanzania, and Zambia, RPR tests were used. The introduction of POCTs was effective across diverse healthcare settings, and their integration into existing healthcare systems facilitated increased testing and treatment rates. This led to policy changes in all participating countries, incorporating POCTs into national guidelines. In Uganda, 82% of healthcare workers found POCTs very easy to perform. At sites where RPR was previously used, healthcare workers reported being able to test more patients daily with POCTs. Both Uganda and Zambia experienced a significant increase in antenatal care (ANC) attendance following the introduction of POCTs. Patients appreciated receiving test results and treatment during their first visit, avoiding the need for follow-up visits. Most patients preferred finger-prick testing over venipuncture due to the smaller blood volume required. In Brazil, the indigenous population initially expressed reservations about POCTs due to concerns about positive test results, pain from the finger prick, and treatment-related issues. In rural China, pregnant women from ethnic minorities were less likely to accept testing, perceiving a low risk of syphilis infection. In Peru, laboratory staff initially opposed nurses and midwives performing tasks traditionally reserved for laboratory technicians. Policy-makers expressed concerns about the cost, quality, and performance of rapid syphilis tests (RSTs), as well as past issues with their implementation. However, healthcare workers were motivated by the opportunity to provide better services and ensure safer pregnancies. Patients reported high satisfaction with RSTs due to same-day testing and treatment (STAT), reduced clinic waiting times, decreased travel time, and improved case detection and treatment rates. Barriers to routine syphilis screening included healthcare providers' perception that syphilis in pregnancy was less important than other diseases, particularly in rural areas. Poor communication between healthcare workers and pregnant women was linked to a lack of routine training, with most healthcare workers receiving only basic training on syphilis management during their professional education. Community-level barriers included the cost of testing, stigma surrounding sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and the role of husbands or partners in approving or supporting the cost of screening. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines emphasize the importance of syphilis screening and treatment for pregnant women to prevent mother-to-child transmission (MTCT). Syphilis is a systemic disease caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum, which can be transmitted congenitally or acquired through sexual contact or blood transfusion. The WHO's global initiative aims to eliminate MTCT of syphilis by ensuring that at least 95% of pregnant women are screened and appropriately treated. Rapid POCTs, including on-site RSTs and RPR tests, are effective tools for syphilis screening. RSTs detect both current and past infections, while RPR tests can indicate active infection and monitor treatment response. These tests can be used as standalone diagnostics or in a sequential manner, where a positive result on the first test leads to confirmatory testing and treatment. Studies have shown that syphilis screening and treatment during pregnancy are cost-effective. However, challenges remain in ensuring high coverage of antenatal syphilis screening and treatment, particularly in resource-limited settings. Barriers include the availability of validated, easy-to-use testing methods and the debate over the suitability of RPR as the screening test of choice due to its time-intensive nature and laboratory requirements. The integration of syphilis screening into ANC services has been shown to improve coverage and patient outcomes. Patients prefer receiving syphilis testing at the same location as ANC services, allowing for STAT and related counseling. However, services provided at different locations or those requiring follow-up visits for results and treatment have lower coverage rates. Addressing these barriers and ensuring consistent availability of resources, training, and quality assurance are critical for scaling up integrated syphilis screening and treatment services.
